`

Tested (full negatives ledger)

Every derivation row uses tools/oracle.py: a candidate only counts as a match if the derived ETH address equals the winner wallet 0x635739254BDE27d28301f25aD57c3cAC3C3468f3 exactly, under any of the 9 swept BIP44 paths (3 accounts times 3 indexes). Witness: the oracle's own --selftest reproduces the public BIP39 KAT address, a positive control that points the oracle at the KAT's own address, a negative control against the real winner wallet, an invalid-checksum rejection, and the artist's prior solved "Bifurcations" BIP84 vector, before every run below.

Audio channel (the toolbox that solved the artist's prior puzzle, "Bifurcations")

Hypothesis | Space | Method | Result | Witness | Date -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- Spectrogram text, Morse (kick/snare as dash/dot), SSTV (including invert-merge), theme-keyed hex offsets, LSB and bit-plane analysis, RIFF/XMP metadata, mid-side decoding, sub-20Hz content, small and medium ASR, demucs vocal isolation plus ASR, run on all 12 lossless masters | 12 tracks times the full toolbox | the same toolbox that solved "Bifurcations" (2020) | negative on all 12 tracks | yes (the toolbox is confirmed to work, since it is what solved the prior puzzle) | 2026-06-17

This is the first sweep of this puzzle's search space (any version of it) that did not filter by checksum, closing the gap flagged above. It only covers the default path and hours 1,2,3,9,10,11's widened windows -- hours 6 and 7 still only have their original 3-candidate window in this run, and the 9 neighbor-path anti-false-negative sweep (--neighbor-paths) has not been run yet.

Building the GPU harness surfaced its own bug worth recording: the first version's mid-sweep "witness" was built from this puzzle's own candidate pool (last candidate of each hour, cw_from_1 order) rather than a fixed external KAT. With --extra that witness is itself a legitimate member of the swept space -- itertools.product emits the all-last-candidate combination last, so the witness necessarily reappeared near the end of the enumeration and tripped a "corrupted target" assertion. Not a GPU/kernel bug: the kernel correctly found it both times. Fixed by using a fixed BIP39 KAT ("abandon"x11 "about", an address that cannot arise from this puzzle's word lists) as the continuously-reinjected canary instead, and by checking the real-target hit before any canary assertion so a real match is never masked by one.

Explicitly not fed to the oracle

Sung lyrics on 2 tracks (DiscomfortMeditation, ShadowRealm) contain several BIP39 wordlist tokens among their ordinary lyrics. I did not test any permutation of these: no mechanism selects which 12 of the many lyric tokens would be the seed or in what order, so testing them would be an unbounded search with no stopping rule, not a bounded hypothesis. This is listed as untested, not as a negative.

Summary

Across the POAP-image family, 1,193,373 plus 531,441 times 4 plus a sampled 8.6e8-sized space have been checked, 0 matches, 0 partial hits. The clock-and-grid mechanism itself (order from the hour position, word from the wordlist cell the numeral overlays) is confirmed by 3 hours that read with no row ambiguity at all; what remains open is resolving the row for the other 9 hours past plus-or-minus 1, which the published 2004-pixel raster does not resolve further.

title: New puzzle: Path to Greatness, 3.03 LTC uploaded
body:
A new open puzzle joins the mid tier: **Path to Greatness: Treasure Hunt**, 3.02608794 LTC (about $164) at `LUtL7qnm3gzxKjHcfVLSjydqhhinTVmTmS`, funded since 2021 and never spent (8 incoming transactions, 0 outgoing, checked 2026-09-12 on litecoinspace.org).

Why this one is worth an afternoon:

- **The author published his own architecture.** A fake desktop screenshot in the game shows the encrypted WIF, four AES-256-CBC segments, their four IVs (album track titles), which clue pairs with which, and the exact length of each of the eight answers. Nothing about the mechanism is left to guess.
- **Four independent locks instead of one.** The 32-byte key is cut into 4 segments of 8 bytes, each encrypted separately. Any guess on one pair of clues is refuted alone, in microseconds, with a false positive rate of 2^-64. You do not need the other six answers to make progress.
- **Certified oracle included.** `tools/oracle.py --selftest` reproduces the author's schema and the witness protocol; `--segment N a b` checks one pair; the full mode turns 8 answers into the WIF and the address.
- **Real findings to build on.** The hidden image in Ship.png is a frame from Titanic (1997), the "will founder" scene (TinEye + FaceNet). The clue 6 melody is the opening of the author's own YouTube track, 15 notes measured to the cent. The chess position, the wasd pointer graph and the km/mi torches are mapped.
- **What I could not do:** about 1.5e13 witnessed pairs across the four segments, 0 match. The ledger says exactly which readings are dead, so you start where I stopped. Segment 1 (the melody plus the "Imagine" date) is the closest.

Also in this PR: Litecoin support in the tooling (schema, validator, escrow checker via litecoinspace.org, index totals).

title: SOLVED: bitcoin-movie-enigma-100ksats
body:
The Bitcoin Movie Enigma prize is solved and claimed. The payout confirmed in block **965998** (2026-09-08 UTC / 2026-09-07 America/New_York).

- Escrow: `bc1q94ecsn0qk8lap2gefrycnms3ruepy889z969a6`
- [Confirmed payout](https://mempool.space/tx/bd3b088164ae32458b97b917af8fab14056461c5e954499f7bd4cf3a67d6c5f4): **99,766 sats**, with a **234-sat fee**.
- Solver: @rabbidbird. Thanks to the contributors in #9 for reconciling the film identities.

The ten intruders are **1, 3, 8, 12, 14, 19, 21, 26, 32, 34**. Each of five thematic groups has two outliers: Kubrick films, 1979 releases, Jean Reno appearances, films lasting at least two hours, and second installments. The Kubrick films belong in the answer; they are not themselves intruders.

For each retained title, remove a leading A/The and expand its opening prefix to the corresponding English BIP39 word. Four letters work where a matching prefix exists; otherwise the three-letter prefix is unique. In panel order:

```
path mad alien apology escape spare miss goddess leopard crime visit clock start first blade guard close barrel term screen matrix toy ghost shine
```

The significant oracle bug: **this phrase has an invalid BIP39 checksum**. Its encoded checksum byte is **47**, but its entropy requires **119**. It still produces the exact escrow address using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512, 2048 rounds, salt `mnemonic`, an empty passphrase, then BIP84 **m/84'/0'/0'/0/0**. Do not repair the last word.

The address was independently reproduced with a manual BIP32/secp256k1/Bech32 implementation. The confirmed transaction's witness uses the same public key. This explains why checksum-filtered searches discarded the answer.

I have prepared the solved-tier move, full title/word mapping, corrected oracle with an actual-solution regression, and payout verification for a PR. No unclaimed recovery material is being disclosed.

The folder README already says: "I believe, without having confirmed it, that the small blob gates `1GSMG...` and the 'Dualite' blob gates `17ucy...`; nothing published states this explicitly". Under `docs/methodology.md` ("A prize is only as real as the mechanism that pays it out") the 3.75 BTC belongs in `addresses[]`, not in `prize.amount`, as the catalogue already does for teikhos contract AEC7 and the fe-lang registry.

## On chain

| date | block | txid | spent from 1GSMG | to 17ucy | change to 1GSMG | locktime |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2020-05-11 | 630,001, first block after the halving | `2aa9a4a9` | 5.00001366 | 2.5 | 2.49815966 | 629,998 |
| 2024-04-24 | 840,725 | `88cdb3cd` | 2.50352132 | 1.25 | 1.253243 | 840,003 |

Full txids: `2aa9a4a90be819d5122d70c993280785a0508f163521e7b38cebb4db0b071b13`, `88cdb3cdca12b471551b1b26188508a14ca5fd8a415223ffb7c190381c9b9df3`.

In the same block 630,001, vanity address `3GSMG24TujqfMJG1kQoBX18DzJHQLeJYMK` sent `a798905f53fdcadcbd2e2a1e61d23ba69a07e26130a78c76da4bf4d7a170f383` (`OP_RETURN 48616c76696e67`, "Halving", plus 700 sat to `1GSMG`), and the split spent that 700-sat output as its third input. Same block, same control.
- The 2024 transaction was built after the halving (locktime 840,003), broadcast on 2024-04-20 per the creator's same-day message (24638 below), and confirmed four days later.

## Creator statements

Telegram message ids and dates below; the group has no stable URL but is searchable by id. "Price" is his word for the prize money. Emoji omitted.

- Announcement from April 2019 in GSMG's main channel, reposted by members (28297, 30565, 43995, 57405; a screenshot of it is dated 2019-04-21 by 57407) and confirmed by the creator (5368, 2021-01-08, in a thread about the next halving: "We mentioned this at the beginning, when the puzzle started."): "We've decided to half the reward on BTC block 630000 and half it further on every next 210000 blocks. So at approx. 24 May 2020 01:49:11 2.5 BTC will be removed from the puzzle address etc etc."
- 5069, 2020-11-25: "We have our reasons halving the price money at every bitcoin halving event"
- 5365, 2021-01-08: "It'll be split on the next halving."
- 8364, 2023-01-13, replying to "Why 5 btc? Was the half (2.5 btc) transferred to another puzzle address? And the solver could receive prizes from both addresses...": "Every btc halving the price will half too."
- 24638, 2024-04-20: "16$ fee. Damn. Well, anyway, see you in 4 years!"

Outside Telegram, the puzzlehunt/gsmgio-5btc-puzzle README, line 18, agrees: "The creator of the puzzle intended to halve the prize each time Bitcoin halving occurs" (its 2.5 BTC figure predates the 2024 halving).

## What points the other way

The creator has not clarified the second address.

- 3923, 2020-05-12: "who knows what you'll find after opening the 2nd door. The price is in half, but what does it mean"
- 8360, 2023-01-12: "the remaining 2.5 btc is well deserved... Or 5, who knows." Asked directly (8365) whether `17ucy` is available to the solver, he pointed at another member's "Who knows..." (8368).
- 66593, 2026-07-13: 'The "5" btc was never the actual prize. That was only a tiny fraction.'
- 9159, 2023-08-06: a member asked whether the halving reduces one address or both; no answer.
- The decoded puzzle text reads "IN CASE YOU MANAGE TO CRACK THIS THE PRIVATE KEYS BELONG TO HALF AND BETTER HALF AND THEY ALSO NEED FUNDS TO LIVE" (in the group as a photo on 2020-05-09, two days before the first split).

None of these says that `17ucy` pays out, or how. The confirmed prize is the `1GSMG` balance. `17ucy` is unconfirmed either way, which is the "not part of the live prize" case the catalogue already labels on aoi-nakamoto stage 1 and ballet AA007448.

## Proposed change

1. `puzzle.json` and `puzzles.json`: `prize.amount` 1.2563451, `usd_estimate` 79,150 (the same 63,000 USD/BTC the current `usd_snapshot` implies; `validate.py` pins the snapshot date to the root), plus a note: the prize halves at every Bitcoin halving (5, 2.5, 1.25 BTC); the 3.75 BTC at `17ucy` was moved out under that rule, has no published payout path, and the reading that the Dualite blob gates it is unconfirmed.
2. `17ucy` entry: keep `role: escrow` (no better enum value), label "halving split-off, creator controlled; second-prize reading unconfirmed, not part of the live prize".
3. Folder README title and "Prize" row: "1.2563451 BTC" with the `[OPEN]` badge, plus one sentence on the 3.75 BTC; same hedge in the "What remains" row and in `difficulty_note`.
4. Top-level README: the hand-edited starter row "up to 5 BTC" to "1.25 BTC"; the generated table, totals block and prize map follow from `build_index.py` and `fig_readme_totals.py`.

The puzzle stays in the big tier (>= $10,000). Happy to send a PR if you agree with the reading.

title: guntis-vitolins-metamask-8-6eth: reading-order model swept and closed, leads re-ranked, one author attribution corrected
body:
This covers the guntis-vitolins-metamask-8-6eth folder only. Per CONTRIBUTING it
is a rule-out plus several leads, so it is a pull request rather than an issue.
It is one PR rather than two because the lead re-ranking is a direct consequence
of the rule-out and reads oddly on its own. Happy to split it if you would
rather review the tested.md row separately.

## What was ruled out

A complete reading-order model over the full recovered 2020 text, not just the 5
planted sentences.

Hypothesis: all 12 elements are whole words written in the recovered 2020
surfaces, 6 per side, keeping written order, with `dutch` at 1, `fog` at 5 and
`parrot` at 12. `fork` is treated as a floater with no reading-order slot,
because it exists only in the post tag "ethereum fork", which is also why hint 5
singles it out and not `fiber`.

Space, as a closed form:

```
video word sets   = C(25,2)*C(2,2) + C(25,3)*C(2,1) = 300 + 4,600 = 4,900
templates         = C(3,2)*C(6,2) = 45   for the (2 pre-fog, 2 mid) shape
                    C(3,3)*C(6,1) = 6    for the (3 pre-fog, 1 mid) shape
video pairs       = 300*45 + 4,600*6 = 41,100
post word sets    = C(18,3) = 816
fork slot choices = 5
arrangements      = 41,100 * 816 * 5 = 167,688,000
checksum-valid    = 10,484,919
result            = 0 match
```

Certification, in the terms AGENTS.md section 9 asks for. The enumerated
arrangement count equals the closed form exactly, in each of the 7 novelty bands
separately and in total, with 0 duplicates across units. The observed checksum
pass rate is 6.254 percent against the predicted 6.25, which is the independent
check that the enumeration and the checksum filter agree. The derivation engine
was validated by known-answer test before and after, `abandon` 11 times plus
`about` deriving `0x9858EfFD232B4033E47d90003D41EC34EcaEda94`, on 2 separate
engines, with 0 disagreements over the run. A synthetic witness was planted in
every unit that could hold one and recovered through the identical pipeline: OK
1,062, SKIP 2,202, NONE 0. So this is a CERTIFIED NEGATIVE, not an assumed one.

A second, smaller sweep extends the same model to substrings, 582,725
derivations, 0 match. That one is explicitly labelled as not closing the
substring lead, since it only covers the reading-order corner of it.

New script, `tools/sweep_reading_order.py`. Stdlib for enumeration and the
checksum filter, derivation delegated to the folder's own `tools/oracle.py`. It
takes the wordlist by argument or environment rather than vendoring it.
`--size` prints the closed form and checks the layout enumeration against it,
`--selftest` verifies the wordlist digest, measures the checksum acceptance rate
on a real unit, and plants a candidate then requires the pipeline to recover it.
`--run` is resumable and flushes per unit. On a hit it writes the phrase to a
file and does not print it.

One caveat stated plainly: the script's in-run witness re-derives through the
same engine, which is weaker than the 2-engine cross-check the original run
used. That is documented in the function itself rather than glossed over.

## Why this changes the lead ranking

Reading order was the assumption that made the challenge searchable. Dropped,
over the same pool and the same 3 anchors:

```
C(38,4) * C(82,3) * 9! = 73,815 * 88,560 * 362,880 = 2.3722x10^15 arrangements
                                                   = 1.4826x10^14 derivations
                                                   = 5.9 years at 792,000/second
```

The 2 existing sweep leads, liaisons and substrings, are together about 0.2
percent of that. They are still worth running because they are hours rather than
years, but they are no longer plausibly where the answer sits, and the remaining
99.8 percent is not purchasable. So the binding constraint moves from search to
word identification, and the leads are re-ordered to put reading first.

Also included, as evidence rather than a conclusion: inside the reading-order
model, `fog` at 5 and `parrot` at 12 with order preserved force the 4 free video
words to split k before `fog` and m between `fog` and `parrot` with k+m=4. Only
`lake` and `also` lie in that middle range, so m is at most 2, forcing (k,m) to
be (2,2) or (3,1), which forces at least 1 of `lake` and `also` into the phrase.
That whole space is now negative. So either the pool is incomplete on the video
side or order is not preserved. Lead 1 is the cheaper of the 2 to test.

## New lead, ranked first: the text shown on screen in the challenge video

In the challenge video at 5:22 to 5:38 the author says the words "could be you
know written in the video on the screen so read carefully". The written rules in
the hint 5 description agree, listing "description, tags, title, video basically
could be anywhere in this video".

Every sweep in tested.md, including mine, draws its pool from the description,
title, tags and post body. No frame of the video image has been read. That is a
different kind of gap from an unswept corner of a pool that has been read.

There is a concrete reason to expect payload there. The video shows a portfolio
table of holdings, and 10 coin names visible or audible in that segment are
BIP-0039 dictionary words: `atom`, `link`, `dash`, `cash`, `icon`, `wave`,
`gas`, `ocean`, `fetch`, `ripple`. Checked against the 2048-word list, none of
the 10 appears in any recovered 2020 written surface. If even 1 is a list
element, every negative in this folder was drawn from an incomplete pool.

Method for anyone with the video: sample frames at 1 per second, read the text,
intersect with the wordlist, add anything new before re-running. Worth checking
explicitly for `cloud`, which decides established fact 3.

I could not do this myself. My environment has no video download and no optical
character recognition available, and I am not going to route around that. It is
about an hour of ordinary desktop work for someone who can.

## New lead: derivation paths

Every sweep in the folder derives only `m/44'/60'/0'/0/0`. The escrow is stated
to be MetaMask, so that is the right first guess, but if it is the second
account of the same wallet then every negative here is a negative about the
wrong address. Re-checking the already-enumerated survivors at
`m/44'/60'/0'/0/1`, `m/44'/60'/0'/0/2`, `m/44'/60'/1'/0/0` and
`m/44'/60'/2'/0/0` costs about 28 percent of the original derivation work,
because the seed stretch is already done and only the child derivation repeats.
Cheapest decisive experiment currently available in the folder, and never run.

## A correction to an author attribution

This is the part I would most like checked, because it changes an existing lead
rather than adding one.

`analysis/leads.md` lead 2 currently says the author, asked whether a list word
could hide inside a longer written word, "answered yes and gave "possible"
inside its own negation, formed with the prefix "im-", as his own example".

Reading the comment thread directly, that example belongs to the reader who
asked the question, not to the author. The author's reply in full is:

> "1. Yes for example usa could be united states in hints , but wikk have corect
> word in text at chalange. 2 no it doeesnt. 3 it coukd be in any positon from 12
> seed"

His own example is "usa" for "united states", which is an abbreviation, he
offers it about hints, and he contrasts it with the challenge text, which "wikk
have corect word". A second thread has the same shape: asked how the first word
can be "Netherlands" when that is not in the wordlist, he replies "It not
necceseraly need to be exact word if you would read a post you would figure it
our exact word."

Read together the 2 replies describe hints that gloss a word, not text that
conceals one inside another. So the substring mechanism is a reader's hypothesis
the author did not contradict, which is weaker than an author-stated mechanism.
I demoted the lead rather than killing it, and added a second argument against
it: all 5 confirmed list words are whole tokens, none is a substring, which has
probability roughly 0.065 under a simple independent model. I also red-teamed
that argument in the file, because the 5 known words are exactly the ones he
wrote hints for and a hint is easier to write for a whole word, so the sample is
not random.

Both replies are now quoted verbatim in `clues/author-posts.md`, replacing the
paraphrase, so a future reader can judge the attribution without going back to
the comments.

## Smaller corrections

Established fact 3 moves from "`fog` or `cloud`, not settled" to `fog`.
Narrowing hint 3 from "related to water" to its actual wording, condensed water
droplets, leaves `fog`, `cloud` and `vapor`; `vapor` is the gas phase; of the
remaining 2 only `fog` is written anywhere, at index 25 of the video
description. Reservation stated in the file: `cloud` becomes live again if it
turns out to be legible on screen.

The sentence "The text of both the video description and the blog post is
confirmed unchanged since 2020 ... byte for byte" is narrowed. The planted
sentences, title and tags are unchanged, but the description's contact address
was edited from an "info@" form to a "guntis@" form and the rules block grew
with each new hint. Those edits are outside the payload, but somebody diffing
the live page against the archive will hit them and should not read them as
tampering.

## What I did not do

No transcript, article text, forum content or wordlist is added. The new data
file is a derived index of which dictionary words appear in which source range
in written order, 46 words, which is the minimum the script needs to reproduce
the sweep. If you would rather it were computed at runtime from a link, say so
and I will change it.

No absolute paths in any script or document. `python3 tools/validate.py --folder
1-big-prizes/guntis-vitolins-metamask-8-6eth` passes locally for every check
group except the oracle self-test, which cannot run in my environment because
`bip_utils` is not installable there. That is an environment limit, not a change
to `tools/oracle.py`, which is untouched. Please confirm check 11 passes on your
side.

The escrow was not swept and nothing was broadcast. Balance last checked
8.61254155425694462 ETH.

title: Timeline Paradox Observation: BLM Collage (0.2 BTC)

# Timeline Paradox Observation: BLM Collage (0.2 BTC)

Hi floflo777,

I've been studying your excellent research on the BLM Collage puzzle (Welcome to the Brave New World) and wanted to share an observation that might be relevant.

## The Discovery

While analyzing the puzzle timeline, I noticed something significant:

- **Funding TX:** May 10, 2020 (fcee21d44ee94c09869947c74b61669bf928358e9c2d1699fb075bb6ebf5d043)
- **George Floyd's death:** May 25, 2020
- **Puzzle image posted:** October 2020

The seed/wallet was funded **15 days before** George Floyd's death, and **5 months before** the puzzle image was published.

## Implication

This suggests the image is a **private bijection** (check-step) rather than a generative recipe. The creator had the seed first, then created the image as a verification mechanism.

This means:
- Brute-forcing the image → seed relationship is likely futile without knowing the bijection
- The puzzle design is fundamentally different from "image contains seed" puzzles
- Community anchor-based approaches may be targeting the wrong mechanism

## My Research

I've documented this observation in my public research repository:
https://github.com/NoobSilence/crypto-puzzle-lab

Specifically in:
- `docs/0.2_BTC_FULL_ANALYSIS.md`
- `docs/DEEP_RESEARCH_2026-08-22.md`

I've tested ~4.5M candidates plus community-derived 377B combinations across 15 different attack vectors, all negative.

## Question

Given this timeline paradox, do you think this puzzle is:
1. Solvable only by the creator (who knows the bijection)?
2. Solvable through a mechanism we haven't identified yet?
3. Effectively parked/unsolvable by design?

Would be interested to hear your thoughts.

Thanks for your excellent work on documenting these puzzles — it's been incredibly valuable for the community.

Best regards,
NoobSilence

title: guntis-vitolins-metamask-8-6eth — errors in prior write-up + new source material
body:
## `guntis-vitolins-metamask-8-6eth` — findings + errors that stayed inherited

Working through this puzzle intensively this session. Sharing what turned up so future solvers don't inherit the same errors we did. Full notes in a longer local doc; this issue is the summary.

### Errors in the current write-up (`analysis/tested.md` + `README.md`)

1. **`top`** — cited to *"video title and hook line"*. Case-insensitive grep of the 2020-06-13 Wayback capture of `youtube.com/watch?v=w4mpiuBP_aY` returned zero hits in title or `og:description`. `top` does appear in the wider blog body prose (*"top ten altcoins"*) and in the video description trailer (*"top mining equipment"*), so the word might still be a candidate — but the sourcing statement is wrong. This propagated into `R1` and every downstream sweep.
2. **`finish`** — placed in the R1 pool as a title/hook-line word. `finish` (bare stem) does not appear literally in any authored surface. `finished` (past participle) is in the og:description tagline *"Crypto Winter finished?"*. So `finish` is a morphological derivative (same class as the F6 inflection sweep), not a literal.
3. **`cloud`** — the README explicitly says *"only `fog` and `lake` appear in the source texts"*, then still carries `cloud` as a pos-5 branch on semantic-fit grounds. Direct grep of every 2020 authored surface (blog HTML, main video HTML, main video description) confirms zero authored `cloud` occurrences — the only hits anywhere are modern (post-2023) CDN URLs and YouTube player JS variables. Every sweep with a `cloud` branch doubled compute on a candidate that fails the "correct word in text at challenge" rule Guntis stated in the Hint-5 video comments.
4. **`fork`-absence-treated-as-elimination** — earlier phases OCR'd 216 images to search for `fork`; found none; the null was interpreted as ruling `fork` out. The tag list in blog HTML metadata had it all along (`ethereum fork` tag, unique-to-this-post). Discovered 2026-08-15 per the repo's own timeline.

### Unresolved contradiction not to close

`analysis/leads.md` cites Guntis's own *"'possible' inside 'impossible' via 'im-' prefix"* example as evidence for a substring mechanism. That contradicts the literal-word rule the same source uses elsewhere. Substring families in the repo's own leads (Tier B, Tier C-length candidates) were never swept exhaustively; this session ran substring Tier A (6 candidates including `possible`) and then deprioritized on a judgment call in favor of the literal rule. If the substring mechanism is real, every literal-rule sweep is over-constrained.

### New author quote worth writing down

From `-MeIaPdVJjA` (comment id `Ugz8NxQbpGiZVY4aMlB4AaABAg.96ssUYBoRva96tAygBNjKq`, 2020-08), replying to a question about pool size:

> *"if will have to many words, people can make bot and have easy guess."*

Design constraint stated directly by Guntis: the plant pool is deliberately small. That validates the *"couple added on top"* reading numerically (~14 planted words = 12 seed + 2 decoys) and argues against very-wide pool sweeps.

### New source material recovered this session

- Full YouTube captions for `w4mpiuBP_aY`, `03wXiMczCXk`, `ZjBJKooVmuE` (via yt-dlp with `--write-auto-subs --sub-langs en`). Hint 4 spoken content transcribed verbatim.
- Full YouTube video description of `w4mpiuBP_aY` (the trailer text past the 3 planted sentences — reveals Guntis's *"6 are hidden in this video (description, tags, title, video basically could be anywhere in this video)"* verbatim).
- A **third planted sentence** in the video description, missing from the current repo's clue list: **"Also It is not impossible."** Sits between V1 and V2 in the description. Byte-verified in every Wayback capture 2020-06-13 through 2024-11.
- Hint source-videos mapped: Hint 1 first appears `3DUufb9wBHA` (2020-02-25), Hint 2 in `-MeIaPdVJjA` (2020-03-31), Hint 3 in `635pXfzlzqA` (2020-05-14). Hint 2 spelling evolved `Netherland` → `Netherlands` mid-2020.
- The `..X..` marker in Hint 3 (*"seed word 5 ..X..  is made of..."*) is byte-identical across all 27 instances (exact bytes: `20 2e 2e 58 2e 2e 20 20`, with an intentional double-space after) and unique to that hint. Meaning still unexplained.

### Bottom-line status

- The only word Guntis has ever stated outright as a seed word is `fork`, spelled letter-by-letter at 17:28 in `ZjBJKooVmuE`.
- Three positions are STATED (via hints 1/2/3): pos 12, pos 1, pos 5. The words filling them are INFERRED, not stated.
- No STATED source-text ever contained a definitive decoy count. *"Couple added on top"* is the tightest constraint.
- Comment fetches across 58 videos returned nothing about "solved", "winner", "abandoned"; blog and Twitter show zero challenge references post-2020; Hint 5 was silently dropped from Guntis's resumed template (2023-11 onward, hints 1-4 only re-added). Unresolved signal — could be template inertia, could be more.

### For anyone continuing

I have a longer local file (`kit/FINDINGS.md`) that labels every line STATED / INFERRED / OBSERVED / TRANSLATED, scopes every session sweep to exactly what it tested, and lists the specific frames that were **killed vs abandoned vs never touched**. Happy to share on request. The one-line rule I'd suggest for any successor: **separate what Guntis said from what someone read into it.**

Not a solver claim — just a records-cleanup so the next person doesn't re-inherit the errors.

body:
## Summary

Creates `analysis/tested.md` and `analysis/leads.md` for a folder that had neither, and
**proposes a reclassification you may want to push back on**: `insight` to `external-info`.

## The reclassification, and why I am flagging it rather than just making it

The folder is rated `insight` on the strength of a note that about 40 to 50 of the 64 hex
characters are legible today. **That figure did not reproduce.** A pass on 2026-08-18
recovered **2 characters** with confidence, and only itag 18 (640x360) is served for all
five videos on that channel, so there is no higher rendition to recover.

If the legible count is nearer 2 than 50, the missing information is 62 of 64 hex
characters, or 16^62. That is a missing-source problem, not a search problem.

The distinction that seems to matter, and the reason I am **not** proposing the same change
for `logicbeach-powerful-moss`: what counts is whether the information lost to the source is
small enough to enumerate. logicbeach names a resolution limit too, but its ambiguity is
about 3 candidates across 9 positions, roughly 19,700, which is trivially searchable. This
one is not. `zden-haluska-halv` is already rated external-info on exactly this basis (118
bits measured against the 256 a key needs), so the precedent exists.

You have far more context on this puzzle than I do, so if the 40-50 figure came from
something I could not see, that is worth knowing and this part of the PR should be dropped.
The rest stands independently.

## The README's rank-1 lead is closed

"Replay Puzzle #1 end to end to fix the reading grammar." Done. Puzzle #1's own answer was
re-derived from its **statement** video (not its solution screen) by residual-vs-temporal-median
plus max projection, reproducing the oracle's known-good vector exactly. That is the witness.

The result is partly negative and worth stating plainly: **the grammar does not transfer.**
Puzzle #1 renders its key directly at low contrast. Puzzle #2 splits single glyphs across the
frame boundary, rotates them, overlays one static decoy glyph, and mirrors part 2. Puzzle #1
certifies the technique, and nothing about the reading rule. Anyone repeating this should not
expect #1 to disambiguate #2's letterforms.

## New structural findings

- **Both seams of part 1 are located.** Frames 610-681 carry one glyph straddling the
  x=0/640 boundary in band y 157-211; frames 728-796 carry one straddling y=0/360 at
  x 297-346.
- **The static decoy is isolated** by its constancy in fixed frame coordinates: from about
  frame 630 its shape stops changing while its peak decays 218 to 72, so it can be
  template-extracted and subtracted.
- **Part 2 contains the literal word `MIRROR`, rendered in mirror image**, alongside two hex
  characters that read `C` and `8` once flipped. That is an explicit instruction from the
  author about how part 2 is read, and it was not recorded anywhere in this folder. It is
  the most actionable thing here.
- **"Composite glyphs" is not quite right.** Each frame carries one glyph, split by the
  frame boundary and reunited by a circular roll; what makes it look composite is the decoy
  overlaying it.
- **The fallback sweep is over-priced.** The README budgets 16^8 if 8 characters remain
  undetermined. The observed ambiguity is pairwise, so k ambiguous cells is 2^k, not 16^k.
  Twenty such cells is about 1.05 million candidates, seconds against the offline oracle.
  The practical consequence is that the read does not have to reach 64 characters before a
  sweep becomes viable, only to the point where every remaining uncertainty is a named
  two-way choice.

## Counts

No 64-hex candidate has been assembled and tested by anyone, so the candidate count against
the escrow stays 0 and `tested_total` records families rather than candidates. The escrow was
re-checked: 0.05 ETH, nonce 0, never signed.

A practical note is included in the file: YouTube now returns HTTP 403 to yt-dlp's default
client for these videos, and `--extractor-args "youtube:player_client=android"` is what works.

## Validation

`python3 tools/validate.py --folder 3-small-prizes/crypto-puzzles-2018-puzzle-2-0-05eth`
passes 15/15.

title: arweave-puzzle-12: 2.86M new negatives, geometry-derived piece 1, heraldic hatching, and a retraction
body:
## Summary

Extends `analysis/tested.md` with rows 7 to 19 and adds `analysis/leads.md`. Cumulative goes
from 156,730 to **3,014,356** assembled 58-character candidates, all negative. Rows 1 to 6
are unchanged.

All sweeps used the folder's own certified oracle. I also added a fast-reject front end
(the `"kty":"RSA"` gate lies wholly in plaintext block 0, so only the first ciphertext block
needs decrypting) which took the rate from 2.04 to 40.3 candidates/second/core. Its scope
limit is documented in the file: it assumes the keyfile begins with `{"kty":"RSA"` at offset
0, as the solved sibling's does.

## Structural findings, measured rather than assumed

**Piece 1's reading order is derived from the image.** The six flag centroids were measured
and group by x into exactly three vertical pairs: left (red `c00000`, purple `410080`),
middle (gray `808080`, green `3f8000`), right (violet `7f00ff`, blank `ffffff`). That turns
the community's "they seem to go in pairs" note into a measurement, and lets twelve
principled reading orders replace 720 arbitrary permutations, cutting the piece-1 space from
4,320 strings to 144 with nothing reasoned lost. It also strengthens Blue independently of
the length budget: exactly one additive primary sits in each of the first two pairs.

**Piece 4 is exactly five letters.** Five hatched squares at 88-89 px, five orange glyphs,
stable across thresholds from <100 to <160. The sixth square-like contour that appears at
looser thresholds is a puzzle-knob shadow at 69x65. The community's six-letter-word
hypothesis (alpine, saline, linear) is refuted: there is no sixth letter.

**The hatching is the Petra Sancta heraldic convention** - each square quartered, each
quadrant hatched in the direction that denotes a tincture (vertical = gules, horizontal =
azure, the two diagonals = vert and purpure). I have not seen this identified anywhere, and
it explains why the hatching is drawn so carefully in four distinct directions rather than
as generic shading. It does **not** order the letters: no single quadrant gives a bijection
(best is 4 distinct of 5), no per-colour count is a permutation of 1 to 5, and reading each
square's four quadrants as a base-4 number under all 24 assignments never yields five
consecutive values. That is an independent second refutation of row 1.

**Flag semaphore is refuted.** Pole angles measure -26.5, 7.7, 17.1, -9.5, 0.2 and 0.2
degrees from vertical; semaphore needs multiples of 45 and the worst deviation is 18.5.

**The author's answer style is broader than row-8-era assumptions allow.** Solved sibling #8
(`RasputinWilhelmAlekhine`) suggests concatenated proper nouns, but sibling #5's confirmed
sub-answers are `*`, `48`, `GCE` and `Eris`, and #3's are four-character tokens including
the chess move `e4d5`. Digit strings and acronyms are in range, so piece 2 need not be a
name at all.

## A retraction, recorded in full

Summing hatch lines per square by threshold profile gave 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17 - five
consecutive integers, which would have ranked the letters L, E, I, N, A. That did not
survive independent measurement. Counting the same lines as connected components gives 12,
12, 11, 7, 11; counting dark runs along a perpendicular scanline gives 7, 15, 11, 13, 6.
Three methods, no agreement, so the hatch-line count is not reliably measurable at this
resolution and the consecutive run was an artifact of one thresholding choice. The ordering
it suggested was tested anyway (row 19) and fails. It is written up as a warning because the
next person will hit the same trap.

## What the negatives close

The 28+18 split is dead across all 24 block orders and all 144 geometry-derived piece-1
orderings, with 137 different 18-character piece-2 readings and both piece-3 forms. That is
the split every solver reaches, because `AndreessenHorowitz` is the only investor name that
closes the budget alone.

Three alternative length branches (12+34, 11+35, 9+37), the hex-encoding branches (36+10
with the date as drawn, 42+4 with `a16z`), the joint-naming model, and the tincture-sequence
reading of piece 4 are all swept and negative. Piece 4 was enumerated over all 120 letter
orders, not just the dictionary anagrams.

`analysis/leads.md` records what remains and, more usefully, what is now closed, so the same
ground is not re-swept.

## Validation

`python3 tools/validate.py --folder 2-mid-prizes/arweave-puzzle-12-400ar` passes 15/15.

title: gsmg.io: tools/oracle.py derives the AES key with the wrong digest
body:
## Summary

`tools/oracle.py` for gsmg.io derives the AES key with `EVP_BytesToKey`/**MD5**. Its
docstring calls MD5 "the scheme used throughout this puzzle's earlier stages". That is not
the case, and it is checkable against the puzzle's own material: the phase-2 and phase-3
blobs decrypt cleanly under **SHA-256** and produce garbage under MD5.

Any candidate previously pushed through this oracle was compared against a key the puzzle
does not produce, so those results are void rather than negative.

## Evidence

Both blobs were re-fetched from the live page and decrypted with their known stage
passwords:

| blob | password | MD5 | SHA-256 |
|---|---|---|---|
| phase 2 | `sha256("causality")` | padding invalid, 35% printable | padding valid, 100% printable, known plaintext ("The ironic 2name of the keymakers...") |
| phase 3 | `sha256(parts 1..7)` | padding invalid, 38% printable | padding valid, 100% printable, known plaintext ("What if the merovingian is wrong...") |

`sha256(parts 1..7)` was recomputed independently and reproduces the published digest
`1a57c572...ec30d5`, which confirms the password string as well as the digest choice.

SHA-256 has been the `openssl enc` default since OpenSSL 1.1.0 (2016); MD5 was the default
only in 1.0.x. The puzzle was published in 2019.

## Why the selftest passed anyway

Part 2 encrypted a self-made blob with the same `evp_bytes_to_key` it then decrypted with.
A round trip certifies self-consistency, not the digest choice, and cannot fail on a wrong
constant used on both sides. It is replaced with the phase-2 blob (real ciphertext, known
password), plus a regression guard asserting MD5 fails on that same blob:

```
HASH160(known on-chain pubkey) -> 1GSMG1JC9wtdSwfwApgj2xcmJPAwx7prBe: OK
phase-2 blob decrypts under sha256("causality"): OK
wrong password on the same blob -> no valid padding: OK
MD5 derivation fails on the same blob (regression guard): OK
published blob shape (96 bytes, salt 3ab585348552415d): OK
SELFTEST OK
```

This also means the README's "no end-to-end known-good vector exists" is too pessimistic:
X is unsolved, but earlier stages provide real blobs with known passwords that certify the
decryption half.

## Scope of the claim

Proven: the shipped digest fails on both blobs in this puzzle whose passwords are known.

Inferred, not proven: that the small blob also requires SHA-256. That cannot be proven
without its password. The inference rests on the same author, the same page family, the
formula the pages print (`aes-256-cbc /w base64 sha-256(password)`), and two independent
confirmations. Stated as an inference in `tested.md` section 10 rather than as a fact.

## Also included

- **`tested.md` section 9**: the first sweeps of the small-blob pipeline, which the ledger
  notes had never been isolated and swept on its own. 1,358,577 candidates, 0 match, run
  under the corrected derivation. Includes the phase-1 form password
  `theflowerblossomsthroughwhatseemstobeaconcretesurface`, recovered from the hidden POST
  form on the `theseedisplanted` page.
- **Location correction**: the small blob is published on the SalPhaseIon page, not on the
  final page reached after the Architect Choice. Verified by reassembling it from that
  page's own single-character token run: the two 64-character halves sit at token
  positions 916 and 1020, separated by 40 `a`/`b` characters that read (a=0, b=1) as the
  five bytes `enter`. This matters for the hunt, because that page's own text decodes to
  `lastwordsbeforearchichoice` and `thispassword`.
- **Lead**: re-run anything previously tested through the shipped oracle.

## Validation

`python3 tools/validate.py --folder 1-big-prizes/gsmg-io-5btc-puzzle` passes 15/15.

Repository-wide, `tools/validate.py` reports 3 failures and 1 warning, but these are
identical on the unmodified tree and none of them names this folder. They are unrelated to
this change.

title: Crypto Puzzles 2018 Part 2
body:
Posting this here in the hope that it might be useful for anyone as stuck as me with this puzzle as I've spent far too much time thinking about it for the tiny amount of ETH in the wallet. 

Here are the steps I did to extract the 9 characters from part 1:

1. yt-dlp the video — 60fps, 1280×720, 1800 frames
2. ffmpeg -ss 20.2 -to 22.2 … -pix_fmt gray → raw frames
3. Threshold 225
4. Each char is split across the screen edges: right 200 cols of frame n + left 200 cols of frame n+19. Anchors [7,9,12,15,17,19,22,24,27]
5. Crop in x only (preserve screen rows), hstack([right,left]), rotate −90°
6. Read as Didot → 6A6B0860B

This method does not render perfectly, but has high confidence score on the characters, so is likely accurate, albeit, needs some slight tweak for it to render perfectly. The B is the main character that doesn't look perfect.

For part 2 of the video, I have not been able to find any way to reconstruct the glyphs into anything meaningful.

Things I've tried: 
**Temporal/stacking** — max/min/median/mean/percentile projection, 95th-pct transient rejection,
per-chunk sub-stacking, σ-map (per-pixel std = full census of every changing pixel).

**Geometric** — edge-clipped reconstruction, split-delay joins, torus roll, y-alignment,
centred joining, mirror-fold (IoU 0.29–0.37), A/B layer shift correlation (peak IoU 0.275,
no snap), hflip whole-frame (scores flat: 0.618 vs 0.620), ±90° rotation, anamorphic/decimation.

**Template matching** — 4 fonts + the setter's own glyph library extracted from Puzzle #1's
solution screen (control validated: known `C`→0.907, known `8`→0.892).

**Signal/frequency** — Difference of Gaussians, 2D FFT, chi-square LSB (Westfeld/Pfitzmann),
DCT coefficient histograms (JSteg/OutGuess detection).

**Audio** — spectrograms, inverted mix, Morse.

**Cross-video** — P1×P2 set ops, mirrored, time-reversed, 1/2/3-frame audio-sync offsets,
temporal mirror blend across **all 400 offsets** (XOR + diff; peak 9 blobs at off=352 vs
baseline 5), side-by-side seam continuity.

**Encoding** — `CRYPTO PUZZLER`+`PART 1`+`MIRROR`+`PART 2` = exactly 32 chars → 64 hex;
all 24 orderings × joiners × cases → 0 matches. Base32 of decoy letters (40 chars = 200 bits,
56 bits short of a key).

**Cryptographic** — ~8.9M key derivations, coincurve-validated against the escrow address.

**Other clues that have me stumped:**

Both video descriptions have deliberate typos. 

Part 1 — "Do you have the intellience to solve the Crypto Puzzle? 0.05ETH is waiting for the best puzzler solver. Is it you?"
  - missing g from intelli**g**ence
  - position in word: 8 (1-based)
  - position in description: 24 (1-based) / 23 (0-based)
  - word 5 of the description; description is 114 chars

  Part 2 — "The first puzzle was solved in hours, so our second is decidely trickier.  Are you smart enough?"
  - missing d from decide**d**ly
  - position in word: 7 (1-based)
  - position in description: 62 (1-based) / 61 (0-based)
  - word 12 of the description; description is 96 chars
  - Double space after trickier. 

'g' occurs EXACTLY ONCE in description 1 — at index 73
  description 2's double space is at index 73 

Anyway, if there are any more insights or progress with decoding any of it please share.

title: Aoi Block 77: writing down the MD5 and the two reimplementation gotchas
body:
Aoi Block 77: writing down the MD5 and the two reimplementation gotchas

Not a new result — the README already says you reproduced Stage One during research (README.md line 145). This is the value written down, plus the two places a reimplementer goes wrong, plus a negative on Real Big Block using the same recipe. Posting in case it saves someone the afternoon it cost me.

The value

source : bitcointalk topic 155054, first post, raw HTML (ISO-8859-1, ASCII body)
md5    : 9dd2efb9bc976c2095bd534d7b8d431c
      -> 19TbyN5KCg1Lg7qHwezifsLVcdSa2Rj5KN   at m/44'/0'/0'/0/0

I couldn't find this hash recorded anywhere in the repo. Having it makes the Stage One reproduction checkable without re-deriving from the post.

The two gotchas

Both are handled correctly in your tools/oracle.py. Neither is stated in the README prose, and both silently produce a wrong hash rather than an error.

1. <br><br> separates paragraphs; a single <br> does not. The post ends ...comfortable with my legacy.<br />[edited slightly] — a single <br />, while every paragraph break is <br /><br />. So [edited slightly] sits inside paragraph 16 behind a newline. It is neither a 17th paragraph nor something to strip:

reading | md5 | result -- | -- | -- 17 paragraphs | 845a41be2cb2017a2cae9104e8fcac47 | no match 16, [edited slightly] removed | dd855d342dea388aa902b4bf94016ea5 | no match 16, kept behind an internal \n | 9dd2efb9bc976c2095bd534d7b8d431c | match

The chapter reproduces the Finney paragraphs with her own edits — facinating -> fascinating, called RPOW -> called Bitcoin. Applying those to the Stage One base in all 32 combinations gives nothing.

On lead 1 (the 2019 browser render): the 12 API pages contain zero empty <p> elements, so the blank lines she describes typing are not in storage at all. I was told Wayback excludes wattpad.com by platform directive and that archive.today holds nothing before 2026 — I could not verify either myself (rate-limited both times), so treat that as unconfirmed rather than established.

A question

Your Guntis tested.md cites 792,000 derivations/s on a rented GPU. I measured a 20-core ARM box at 14,339/s for the same pipeline (PBKDF2-2048 + BIP32 + secp256k1 + keccak) — 55x short, and it's the PBKDF2 that dominates. Is that solver something you'd consider publishing, or can you say what it's built on? If it's Bitcoin-only I'd be glad to contribute the Ethereum path back.

Thanks for the repo — the oracle-first, witness-or-it-doesn't-count rule is what made the <br> thing findable instead of just another failed guess.
